q: What is mental health, and why does it matter?
a: It concerns physical fitness and how much exercise we do.
It shapes how we think, feel, cope, and connect with others.
It describes our intelligence and how quickly we learn things.
It means feeling cheerful and avoiding all unpleasant emotions.
why: Mental health affects how we think, feel, cope and relate to others. It matters in everyday life and does not mean being cheerful all the time.

q: Does struggling with mental health mean someone is weak?
a: It shows how much determination someone puts into solving problems.
It reflects how well someone can manage challenges without support.
It is a human experience that does not define someone’s strength.
It reveals how prepared someone is to handle everyday responsibilities.
why: Mental health difficulties do not define someone’s strength, determination or worth. Needing support is a human experience.

q: What are some common signs of stress?
a: Irritability, muscle tension, and difficulty sleeping or concentrating.
Constant confidence, steady energy, and an increased sense of calm.
Better concentration, relaxed muscles, and consistently restful sleep.
Greater patience, fewer worries, and feeling comfortable under pressure.
why: Stress can affect emotions, the body, sleep and concentration. These signs can have other causes too; a quiz cannot diagnose their cause.

q: Is mental health just as important as physical health?
a: No, physical health always matters more than emotional well-being.
Only when emotional difficulties begin to cause physical symptoms.
Yes, both affect overall well-being and can influence each other.
Only when someone has received a formal mental health diagnosis.
why: Mental and physical health both contribute to overall well-being and can influence each other. Mental health matters even without physical symptoms or a diagnosis.

q: How can you support a friend who is struggling emotionally?
a: Explain that other people have bigger problems to deal with.
Listen without judgment and ask what support would feel helpful.
Encourage them to stay busy so they forget their difficult feelings.
Give them a solution before they finish explaining their situation.
why: Listening without judgment and asking what would help respects your friend’s needs. Comparing problems or rushing into solutions can make it harder to talk.

q: When might someone benefit from professional support?
a: Only when their situation becomes an immediate emergency.
Only after friends and family have tried every possible solution.
When they can no longer manage any of their daily responsibilities.
Whenever they need help, including before difficulties become severe.
why: People can seek professional support before difficulties become severe. They do not need to wait for an emergency or for other forms of support to be exhausted.

q: Where can someone look for mental health support in Vietnam?
a: A hospital, school counsellor, or qualified mental health professional.
A public discussion group where strangers suggest personal treatments.
A social media account that promises the same cure for everyone.
An online personality quiz that recommends treatment from a score.
why: A hospital, school counsellor or qualified mental health professional can be a starting point. The Vietnam helplines below offer additional options for different needs; check each service’s audience and opening hours.

q: What can someone do if their first attempt to get support is unsuccessful?
a: Wait until the problem becomes more serious before trying again.
Assume that other support services will give the same response.
Try another service or ask someone trusted to help them connect.
Decide that an unanswered call means support is unavailable everywhere.
why: An unsuccessful first attempt does not mean all support is unavailable. Try another suitable service or ask someone trusted to help. If someone is in immediate danger, seek emergency medical help rather than waiting for a helpline.
